items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “the permanent removal of forest cover for other land uses”.
items.answer: Deforestation
items.markingKey: Deforestation: the permanent removal of forest cover for other land uses. [1]

items.stem: Explain the causes of tropical deforestation.
items.answer: Cattle ranching, commercial crops (soya, oil palm), logging, mining (Carajás), road building (BR-163), HEP reservoirs, settlement schemes and population pressure; demand from global markets and government policy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per cause with example [4]

items.stem: Explain the environmental impacts of tropical deforestation.
items.answer: Loss of biodiversity and habitats; soil erosion and leaching; reduced evapotranspiration and rainfall recycling; increased flood peaks and siltation; release of carbon contributing to climate change.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per impact [4]

“Economic development is the main cause of tropical deforestation.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Commercial agriculture (cattle, soya, oil palm), logging, mining and HEP, driven by global demand and national development plans. Against: Population pressure and poverty (shifting cultivators, fuelwood), weak governance and land speculation, and climate-related fires also drive loss. Conclusion: Commercial economic activity is now the dominant driver, enabled by government policy and weak enforcement, with poverty playing a smaller role.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “large-scale beef production on cleared land, the main driver of Amazon deforestation”.
items.answer: Cattle ranching

items.stem: A student writes: “Deforestation only has local impacts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It affects global carbon, regional rainfall and global biodiversity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate geographical explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain the causes of savanna degradation.
items.answer: Overgrazing as herds grow; expansion of cultivation; fuelwood collection; changing fire regimes; drought; sedentarisation of pastoralists.

items.stem: Fig. 4.1 shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Legal Amazon (km², PRODES satellite monitoring): 2004: 27 772, 2008: 12 911, 2012: 4 571, 2016: 7 893, 2019: 10 129, 2021: 13 038, 2022: 11 594, 2023: 9 001, 2024: 6 288. Suggest reasons for the rise between 2012 and 2021.
items.answer: Weakened environmental enforcement and budgets, changes to the Forest Code (2012), high beef and soya prices, land grabbing and political signals encouraging clearance.

items.stem: Fig. 4.1 shows annual deforestation in the Brazilian Legal Amazon (km², PRODES satellite monitoring): 2004: 27 772, 2008: 12 911, 2012: 4 571, 2016: 7 893, 2019: 10 129, 2021: 13 038, 2022: 11 594, 2023: 9 001, 2024: 6 288. items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “using an environment to meet present needs without reducing its ability to meet the needs of future generations”.
items.answer: Sustainable management

items.stem: Explain the role of indigenous people in the sustainable management of rainforests.
items.answer: Traditional knowledge, low-impact use (shifting cultivation with long fallows, hunting, gathering), legal land rights that block clearance; e.g. Kayapó territories in Pará.

items.stem: Explain the difficulties of achieving sustainable management in tropical environments.
items.answer: Pressure from commercial interests and global demand; poverty; weak enforcement and corruption; land-rights conflicts; cost of monitoring; competing government priorities.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per difficulty [4]

items.stem: Name a case study of the sustainable management of a tropical environment you have studied. For your example, describe the strategies used to manage the environment sustainably.
items.answer: Costa Rica: National parks and reserves cover about 25% of the land; Payments for Ecosystem Services (PSA, 1997) funded by a fuel tax pay landowners to protect forest; ecotourism (Monteverde, Corcovado); ban on clearing forest (1996 Forestry Law).

items.stem: Name a case study of the sustainable management of a tropical environment you have studied. For your example, evaluate the success of the management.
items.answer: the Danum Valley, Sabah (Malaysian Borneo): Protects biodiversity including orang-utans and provides research data on recovery after logging; but surrounding areas were heavily logged and converted to oil palm; isolated fragments limit wildlife movement.

items.answer: the Danum Valley, Sabah (Malaysian Borneo): Conservation area of primary lowland dipterocarp forest within a larger logging concession; reduced-impact logging trials; research centre; ecotourism lodge; Yayasan Sabah Foundation management.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a named, located example; up to 4 marks for accurate, place-specific points (names, dates, figures), max 2 if general. Named measures, actors, dates, scale. [5]

items.stem: Using a named example of the sustainable management of a tropical environment you have studied, evaluate the extent to which the tropical environment has been managed sustainably.
items.answer: Model answer (Costa Rica): National parks and reserves cover about 25% of the land; Payments for Ecosystem Services (PSA, 1997) funded by a fuel tax pay landowners to protect forest; ecotourism (Monteverde, Corcovado); ban on clearing forest (1996 Forestry Law). Forest cover rose from about 21% in the late 1980s to over 50%; tourism earns several billion US dollars; but some cleared land was low-value pasture anyway, payments are small, and pressures from pineapple and oil palm plantations remain.

An agreement in which part of a country’s foreign debt is cancelled in return for investment in conservation.

items.stem: Explain how certification schemes such as FSC can support sustainable management.
items.answer: Consumers and firms buy certified timber, rewarding producers who log selectively, protect biodiversity and respect local rights; but coverage is small and fraud occurs.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that sustainable management of tropical environments is only possible with international support?
items.answer: For: Funding from the Amazon Fund, REDD+, debt-for-nature swaps and certification markets pays for monitoring and alternative livelihoods. Against: National policies and local action are decisive: Costa Rica’s fuel-tax-funded PES, indigenous land rights, community forestry in Nepal or Mexico; international funding fails without governance. Conclusion: International support helps, but strong national governance and local community benefits are the key requirements.

items.stem: Name the geographical term that matches this definition: “responsible tourism to natural areas that conserves the environment and benefits local people”.
items.answer: Ecotourism

items.stem: Explain the benefits of agroforestry for farmers and the environment.
items.answer: Trees protect soil from erosion, fix nitrogen and add litter; provide fruit, fuel and timber; diversify income; shade crops; store carbon; reduce pressure to clear forest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per benefit [4]

items.stem: Explain how ecotourism can support conservation.
items.answer: Provides income and jobs that depend on intact ecosystems; entry fees fund rangers and research; raises awareness; gives local people an incentive to protect wildlife.

items.stem: In one year, a reserve in Sabah, Malaysia received 20 000 visitors. Each paid an entry fee of US$80 and spent an average of US$500 on accommodation, food and guides. About 45% of this spending leaked out of the local economy. Suggest how the reserve could prevent visitor numbers from damaging the ecosystem.
items.answer: Limit numbers by permit; zoning with trails; trained guides; boardwalks; seasonal closures; monitoring.

items.stem: In one year, a lodge in the Peruvian Amazon received 40 000 visitors. Each paid an entry fee of US$80 and spent an average of US$150 on accommodation, food and guides. About 43% of this spending leaked out of the local economy. (a) Calculate the total income from entry fees. (b) Suggest how the reserve could prevent visitor numbers from damaging the ecosystem.
items.answer: (a) US$3 200 000 (b) Limit numbers by permit; zoning with trails; trained guides; boardwalks; seasonal closures; monitoring.

items.stem: Jonas argues that ecotourism is the most effective strategy for conserving tropical environments. How far do you agree? Support your answer with examples. In your answer you may refer to agroforestry and scale.
items.answer: For: Ecotourism links income to conservation (Costa Rica, Rwanda gorillas, Danum Valley); fees pay for rangers. Against: Ecotourism is small-scale and vulnerable; legal protection, indigenous land rights, agroforestry, REDD+ payments and enforcement against illegal clearance often have larger effects. Conclusion: Ecotourism helps in accessible, scenic areas, but large-scale conservation depends on legal protection and alternative livelihoods across whole landscapes.

items.stem: Explain the limitations of ecotourism.
items.answer: Small scale, so limited income; visitor impacts (trampling, waste, disturbance); flights add carbon; leakage of profits to foreign firms; vulnerable to shocks such as COVID-19.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “ecotourism”?
options: A UNESCO-designated area with a strictly protected core, a buffer zone and a transition zone where people live and work.
Responsible tourism to natural areas that conserves the environment and benefits local people.

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain the benefits of agroforestry for farmers and the environment. (b) A student writes: “Ecotourism has no environmental impacts.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.

items.answer: For: Ecotourism links income to conservation (Costa Rica, Rwanda gorillas, Danum Valley); fees pay for rangers. Conclusion: Ecotourism helps in accessible, scenic areas, but large-scale conservation depends on legal protection and alternative livelihoods across whole landscapes.

items.stem: “Economic development is the main cause of tropical deforestation.” How far do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: For: Commercial agriculture (cattle, soya, oil palm), logging, mining and HEP, driven by global demand and national development plans. items.stem: With reference to a case study of the sustainable management of a tropical environment, evaluate the extent to which the tropical environment has been managed sustainably.
items.answer: Model answer (Costa Rica): National parks and reserves cover about 25% of the land; Payments for Ecosystem Services (PSA, 1997) funded by a fuel tax pay landowners to protect forest; ecotourism (Monteverde, Corcovado); ban on clearing forest (1996 Forestry Law). Forest cover rose from about 21% in the late 1980s to over 50%; tourism earns several billion US dollars; but some cleared land was low-value pasture anyway, payments are small, and pressures from pineapple and oil palm plantations remain.

items.stem: With reference to a case study of the sustainable management of a tropical environment, describe the strategies used to manage the environment sustainably. To what extent is your chosen example typical of the sustainable management of a tropical environment?
items.answer: Model answer (the Brazilian Amazon (PPCDAm and the Amazon Fund)): Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Deforestation (2004): satellite monitoring (DETER), IBAMA enforcement, new protected areas and indigenous lands; soy moratorium (2006); Amazon Fund (2008) financed by Norway and Germany. Deforestation fell by about 80% from 2004 to 2012; rose again to over 13 000 km² in 2021 when enforcement weakened; fell to about 6300 km² in 2024 after policies were restored; illegal mining and land grabbing persist.
